summary: Defines YANG, a data modeling language for configuration and state data that NETCONF manipulates, as well as for NETCONF remote procedure calls and notifications. It lets network device settings be described in a precise, machine-readable way.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG describes the settings, reported state, operations, and event messages that a NETCONF device supports. Its rules let a client and a device interpret the same data in the same way, including which values are valid.

subtitle: A precise way to describe NETCONF data, operations, and events.

tldr.problem: NETCONF messages carry XML, but clients and servers need a shared description of the data, operations, and valid values that a device supports.
tldr.mechanism: YANG defines a model as named nodes arranged in a tree. It adds types, constraints, reusable definitions, optional features, and mappings from the model to NETCONF XML.
tldr.outcome: The model gives a NETCONF client and server a contract for interpreting data and operations. RFC 6020 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9890.

today: RFC 6020 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010, and it is updated by RFC 9890. The unit metadata does not list a document that obsoletes RFC 6020.

sections.title: What YANG Defines
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language for the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF). A YANG module describes configuration and state data, NETCONF remote procedure calls (RPCs), and notifications. It specifies how model data is represented in XML and how NETCONF operations manipulate that data.

The model gives a client and server a shared description of the data they exchange. YANG focuses on NETCONF data models rather than arbitrary XML documents or arbitrary data models. The RFC also says YANG aims, where possible, to remain compatible with SMIv2 models for read-only access.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG describes what data a NETCONF device can send, report, or change. A client and device can use the same model to agree on the names, meanings, and allowed values of that data.

sections.title: The Data Tree
sections.content:
A YANG model organizes data as a tree. A leaf holds one value, such as a string. A leaf-list holds a sequence of values of one type. A container groups child nodes and has no value of its own. A list holds repeated entries, each identified by the values of its key leafs.

The model can also define choices between alternatives. Only one case within a choice may be represented at a time, and the choice and case nodes themselves do not appear in the data tree or NETCONF messages. The RFC's example module puts a hostname, domain-search values, and login information under a system container.
sections.plainLanguage: A YANG model arranges settings and reported values in a tree. A leaf holds one value, a container groups values, and a list holds entries that keys distinguish from one another.

sections.title: Modules and Reuse
sections.content:
A module is YANG's main unit of definition and describes one data model. A module may include submodules, which split its definitions into parts while keeping the outside view as one module. It can import definitions from other modules and include definitions from its own submodules. Circular import or include chains are not allowed.

YANG supports reuse through derived types and groupings. A grouping defines reusable nodes that a uses statement adds to a schema tree, and refine can adjust selected properties. An augment statement adds nodes at a chosen point in a schema tree, including a tree defined by another module. Modules identify their XML namespace and use prefixes to refer to definitions from imported modules.
sections.plainLanguage: A module is a complete model, even when its author splits the definitions into submodules. It can reuse definitions from other modules and add new nodes to an existing model.

sections.title: Readable Syntax and Typed Values
sections.content:
YANG uses a readable syntax similar to C and C++. Modules use UTF-8, and comments can be written as single-line or block comments. A statement ends with a semicolon or contains other statements inside braces. Identifiers are case-sensitive, and implementations must support identifiers up to 64 characters.

Built-in types include signed and unsigned integers, decimal numbers, strings, booleans, enumerations, bits, binary data, references, empty values, and unions. A model can define derived types and restrict values with rules such as range, length, or pattern. For example, the RFC shows a percentage type based on uint8 with a range from 0 through 100. The decimal64 type requires fraction-digits from 1 to 18.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG uses a text format that people can read and tools can parse. Each value has a type, and a model can limit which values that type accepts.

sections.title: Configuration, State, and Operations
sections.content:
The config statement distinguishes writable configuration from state data. Configuration can be read with <get-config> and changed with operations such as <edit-config>. State data is marked config false; it is returned by <get> and cannot be changed with <edit-config>.

A YANG rpc statement defines a NETCONF operation and can describe its input and output data. A notification statement defines the data in an event sent by a server. These definitions use the same data nodes as the rest of a model, and the RFC specifies how they map to XML. YANG does not define a formal mechanism for every circumstance in which a server may change configuration data on its own.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG marks which values a client can change and which values only describe the device's current state. It can also describe the inputs and outputs of an operation, or the information in an event message.

sections.title: Features, Deviations, and Constraints
sections.content:
A YANG model is a contract between a NETCONF client and server. A module can mark parts of its model as optional with feature and if-feature; a device supports only the features it provides. A device can also describe a deviation from a model. The server advertises module, feature, and deviation information in its NETCONF <hello> message.

Constraints define which data is valid. They can limit values, require nodes, or relate one node to another. For configuration, a server checks constraints while parsing RPC payloads, processing NETCONF operations, and validating the resulting data. Validation for the running or startup datastore occurs at the end of <edit-config> or <copy-config>; for the candidate datastore it occurs at <commit> or <validate>. The RFC defines NETCONF error responses for several model violations.
sections.plainLanguage: A device reports which optional parts of a model it supports and where it differs from the model. It must also check that data follows the model's rules and return defined errors when data breaks them.

sections.title: Updating a Module Safely
sections.content:
A published module can change only in ways that avoid interoperability problems between clients using an earlier version and servers using the update. Each published change adds a new revision statement. The module name and XML namespace must not change, and obsolete definitions must remain because other modules may still refer to them.

The RFC permits compatible changes such as adding enum values without changing existing values, widening a value range, adding new definitions, and relaxing some constraints. A change that alters the meaning of an existing definition must instead use a new definition with a new identifier. This rule lets a module evolve without silently changing the meaning of its existing data.
sections.plainLanguage: A module update must preserve the meaning of existing definitions so older clients and updated servers can still interoperate. If a change would give an existing definition a new meaning, the model must use a new name.

sections.title: The XML Form Called YIN
sections.content:
YIN is an XML-based notation for the same information that a YANG module contains. Each YANG keyword has a corresponding YIN element, and the YIN document's root is a module or submodule element. A statement's argument appears either as an XML attribute or as a child element, according to the mapping defined by the RFC.

YANG and YIN carry equivalent model information, so tools that work with XML can process YIN. Translating between the formats does not preserve comments or whitespace, but it does not change the model's information content.
sections.plainLanguage: YIN writes a YANG model as XML while keeping the same model information. This lets XML tools process the model, although comments and whitespace do not survive translation.

sections.title: Names and File Formats
sections.content:
The RFC creates the IANA registry named YANG Module Names. It records module or submodule names and their associated information, including a module's XML namespace and prefix or a submodule's parent module. There were no initial assignments. Registered names and XML namespaces must be unique; the prefixes ietf- and irtf- are reserved for IETF and IRTF stream documents.

The RFC registers XML namespaces for YANG and YIN and media types for their files. YANG uses application/yang with the .yang extension. YIN uses application/yin+xml with the .yin extension.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA records module names so registered names and XML namespaces stay unique. The RFC also registers names for YANG and YIN XML namespaces and media types for their files.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the YANG language itself has no security impact on the Internet, but models, RPCs, and notifications may contain or transfer sensitive information. The documents that define particular models and the interfaces used to access them must address the security of that information. Its protection depends on the transmission infrastructure, applications that store or release the data, and adequate authentication and access control.

The RFC also warns that YANG parsers must handle malformed documents robustly. Reading a malformed document from an unknown or untrusted source could let an attacker gain the privileges of the parser's user. In an extreme case, the attack could compromise the entire machine.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG does not protect sensitive information by itself. Systems must protect the data and access to it, and parsers must safely handle malformed model files from untrusted sources.
